prompt: Two different book objects were used as keys of a plain object. Why did `Object.keys(loans)` list one key?
hint: What type is a property name?

choices.text: Both became the string `"[object Object]"`
choices.why: Right. Property names are strings, so the second overwrote the first.

choices.text: Plain objects keep only their most recent key
choices.why: An object keeps every property; these two had the same name.

choices.text: The second book was a copy of the first, so they matched
choices.why: They had different titles; the conversion to text made them equal.

choices.text: `Object.keys` skips keys that are objects
choices.why: There were no object keys left to skip.

prompt: Counting words with a plain object, the word `constructor` started from a function instead of zero. Why?
hint: Where did that property come from?

choices.text: `constructor` is a reserved word in JavaScript
choices.why: It is allowed as a property name; the object already had one.

choices.text: `||` turns strings into functions
choices.why: It returned the left side, which was already a function.

choices.text: It was already there, inherited
choices.why: Right. Lesson 8 explains inheritance; a `Map` has no such names.

choices.text: The loop visited the word twice
choices.why: It appears once in the list.

prompt: `loans.set(1, "the number one"); loans.set("1", "the string one");` How many entries do those two lines make in a `Map`?
hint: How does a `Map` compare keys?

choices.text: One, because `1` and `"1"` are the same key
choices.why: That is what a plain object would do.

choices.text: Two: `1` and `"1"` differ under `===`
choices.why: Right. `get(1)` and `get("1")` gave different values.

choices.text: None, because a `Map` refuses number keys
choices.why: Any type of key is accepted.

choices.text: One, and the second line throws
choices.why: No error; both were stored.

prompt: `JSON.stringify(prices)` where `prices` is a `Map` printed `{}`. What should the code do before sending it?
hint: JSON knows objects and arrays.

choices.text: Nothing: an empty object means the prices were zero
choices.why: The prices were dropped, not zero.

choices.text: Use a `Set` instead, which JSON does support
choices.why: A `Set` is dropped the same way.

choices.text: Call `JSON.stringify` twice
choices.why: The second call would stringify the string `"{}"`.

choices.text: Convert it with `Object.fromEntries(prices)`
choices.why: Right, when the keys are strings.

prompt: To loop over a `Map` and get each entry as a `[key, value]` pair, write `for (const [key, value] ___ loans)`.
hint: The same loop works on arrays.

prompt: What is the usual one-line way to remove duplicates from an array `list`?
hint: A `Set` holds each value once.

choices.text: `list.filter(Set)`
choices.why: `Set` is a constructor; calling it without `new` throws.

choices.text: `[...new Set(list)]`
choices.why: Right. Build the set, spread it back into an array.

choices.text: `new Set(list).length`
choices.why: A `Set` has `size`, not `length`, and that is a count, not the items.

choices.text: `list.unique()`
choices.why: Arrays have no such method.

prompt: What was the size of `new Set([NaN, NaN, 0, -0])`?
hint: A `Set` treats `NaN` as equal to itself.

prompt: `new Set([{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]).size` is 2. Why?
hint: Lesson 2 compared objects.

choices.text: A `Set` ignores objects when it removes duplicates
choices.why: It compares them, by identity.

choices.text: `id` is a reserved property, so the two differ
choices.why: `id` is ordinary; what differs is which object it is.

choices.text: They are two objects, however alike
choices.why: Right. Objects are the same only if they are the same object.

choices.text: The second object was added after the first was deleted
choices.why: Nothing was deleted.

prompt: Match each operation on `ana` and `bia` with what it returned.
hint: Union is everything, intersection is shared.

prompt: A program checks `blocked.includes(id)` for every request against a list of 50,000 blocked ids. What does the section suggest?
hint: Which lookup stays fast as the collection grows?

choices.text: Sort the array so `includes` stops sooner
choices.why: `includes` still checks item by item from the start.

choices.text: Use `find` instead of `includes`
choices.why: `find` walks the array the same way.

choices.text: Build a `Set` once and ask `has`
choices.why: Right. `has` does not slow down as the set grows.

choices.text: Use a `WeakSet`, since ids are small
choices.why: A `WeakSet` takes objects only, and ids are numbers or strings.

prompt: By the section's test, when should a dictionary be a `Map` rather than an object?
hint: Where do the keys come from?

choices.text: When there are more than ten keys
choices.why: The test is about where keys come from, not how many.

choices.text: When the keys come from the data
choices.why: Right. Keys written in the source are an object's.

choices.text: When the values are numbers
choices.why: The values do not decide it.

choices.text: When the data will be sent as JSON
choices.why: That is the case where an object is easier to send, and it converts in one line.

prompt: Match each job with the collection the section's table gives for it.
hint: One row each.

pairs.left: A book's title, author and year
Look up a reader by an id from the database
Know whether a tag was already shown
Mark page elements already set up

prompt: `const byId = new Map(books.map((b) => [b.id, b]));` What does `byId.get(12)` replace?
hint: The section's last paragraph.

choices.text: A `filter` that keeps one book
choices.why: That is close, and the section names a different method.

choices.text: A `find` that walked the whole array
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A call to `Object.keys` on every book
choices.why: That lists names; it does not look a book up.

choices.text: A `Set` of ids
choices.why: A `Set` would say whether an id exists, not return its book.

prompt: What happened when `weakmap.js` called `visits.set("ana", 1)`?
hint: What kind of key does a `WeakMap` accept?

choices.text: The string was turned into an object and stored
choices.why: Nothing was stored; it threw.

choices.text: `TypeError: Invalid value used as weak map key`
choices.why: Right. Keys must be objects.

choices.text: It replaced the entry for `reader`
choices.why: `"ana"` and the object `reader` are different keys, and the call threw anyway.

choices.text: It was ignored, as `size` was `undefined`
choices.why: `size` is missing because a `WeakMap` has none; the call itself threw.

prompt: Why can a `WeakMap` not be looped over or counted?
hint: The entries can disappear.

choices.text: Looping was planned, but no engine has built it yet
choices.why: It is left out on purpose.

choices.text: Its keys are secret for security reasons
choices.why: The reason is the collector, not secrecy.

choices.text: Its entries vanish when the collector decides
choices.why: Right: the collector decides when.

choices.text: It holds only one entry at a time
choices.why: It holds as many as you set.

prompt: In `private.js`, why did `console.log(acc)` print `{ owner: 'ana' }` without the balance?
hint: Where is the balance stored?

choices.text: It is stored beside the object, not on it
choices.why: Right. Only code that reaches the `WeakMap` can read it.

choices.text: `console.log` hides numeric properties
choices.why: It prints every property; the balance is not one.

choices.text: The balance is zero, and zero is not printed
choices.why: The balance was 2490, as the same line shows.

choices.text: `deposit` deleted the property after adding to it
choices.why: `deposit` never touched the object.

prompt: In `countObjects`, what is the `WeakSet` called `seen` for?
hint: The book's author points back at the book.

choices.text: Counting the objects, through its `size`
choices.why: A `WeakSet` has no `size`; `n` counts.

choices.text: Holding the results so they can be printed
choices.why: The result is the number returned.

choices.text: Marking objects already visited
choices.why: Right. The book was reached twice.

choices.text: Making the objects immutable while counting
choices.why: A `WeakSet` does not change its members.

prompt: How many objects did `countObjects(book)` find?
hint: The book, the author, and one array.

prompt: A page keeps a `Set` of every element it has initialised, and elements are removed and added all day. What goes wrong that a `WeakSet` avoids?
hint: Who keeps a removed element alive?

choices.text: The `Set` stops accepting elements after a thousand
choices.why: A `Set` has no such limit.

choices.text: Removed elements are initialised twice
choices.why: The mark is still there, so they would not be.

choices.text: A `Set` cannot hold elements, only strings
choices.why: It holds any value.

choices.text: Removed elements stay in memory
choices.why: Right. The `WeakSet` lets them go.

prompt: When does the garbage collector reclaim an object?
hint: The rule the section starts with.

choices.text: As soon as its variable goes out of scope
choices.why: Something else may still point at it, as the `Map` did.

choices.text: When the program calls `delete` on it
choices.why: `delete` removes a property; it does not free an object.

choices.text: Some time after nothing reachable points at it
choices.why: Right, and when exactly is the engine's choice.

choices.text: Every second, on a timer
choices.why: The engine decides, and not on a fixed clock.

prompt: In `weak-gc.js`, why was the object stored as a `Map` key still there after `gc()`?
hint: Its variable had been set to `null`.

choices.text: `gc()` only collects objects created after it was enabled
choices.why: Both objects were created the same way.

choices.text: The `Map`, still in use, pointed at it
choices.why: Right. A `Map` counts; a `WeakMap` does not.

choices.text: `WeakRef` kept it alive
choices.why: A `WeakRef` keeps nothing alive; it collected the other one.

choices.text: Its title was longer
choices.why: Size of contents has nothing to do with reachability.

prompt: To call `gc()` from a script in the lab, Node was started with the flag `--expose-___`.
hint: Two letters.

prompt: What does the section give as the rule for writing code with the weak collections?
hint: If you hold the key...

choices.text: Call `gc()` before reading an entry, so the result is known
choices.why: `gc()` exists only with an experimental flag.

choices.text: Check `size` before every `get`
choices.why: There is no `size`.

choices.text: Reach entries only through a key object you are holding
choices.why: Right. Holding the key keeps the entry.

choices.text: Store a copy of every key in a `Map` as well
choices.why: That keeps every key alive and defeats the purpose.

prompt: A function caches the result of an expensive measurement for each DOM element it is given. Which collection fits?
hint: The keys are objects you do not own.

choices.text: An object keyed by the element
choices.why: Every element would become the same string key.

choices.text: A `Map` keyed by the element itself
choices.why: It works, and keeps every element alive after the page removes it.

choices.text: A `WeakMap` keyed by the element
choices.why: Right. The entry goes when the element does.

choices.text: A `WeakSet` of the results
choices.why: A `WeakSet` has no values, and the results are numbers.

prompt: Put the steps of `countObjects` in the order it runs them for one value.
hint: The checks come before the mark.
items: Return 0 if the value is not an object
Count it and walk its children
trap: Marking after walking the children would let the cycle send the walk round again before the mark exists.
